segments.english: After these things the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision, saying: Do not fear, Abram. I am your shield. Your reward is very great.
segments.literal: after the-things these came word-of the-LORD to Abram in-the-vision saying: not fear Abram; I (am) shield to-you; your-reward great very.

tokens.note: Qatal of הָיָה with דְּבַר (the word) as subject: the word came to Abram. The verse opens with a temporal phrase and no conjunction.
Construct state: 'the word of the LORD'.
ב with the article: 'in the vision'. The English drops the article; the prophetic sense is Ibn Ezra's 'visions of prophecy'.
Infinitive construct with ל: the formula that introduces direct speech.
Jussive after אַל: a prohibition, 'do not fear'.
The parse gives the suffix ךְ as feminine. The addressee is Abram, so the sense is masculine; the vowel of ךְ is the one MAM prints here.
Infinitive absolute in predicate position: 'your reward is great'.

phrases.english: the word of the LORD came to Abram

grammar: הָיָה דְבַר־יְהוָה אֶל־אַבְרָם: the qatal הָיָה has the word of the LORD as its subject, so the speech arrives as an event ('the word came').
לֵאמֹר introduces the speech: an infinitive construct with לְ, the usual formula, rendered 'saying:'.
אַל תִּירָא: negative אַל with a second-person jussive is a prohibition, 'do not fear'.
The etnaḥta on לֵאמֹ֑ר divides the verse between the narration (the word came) and the speech (Do not fear ...).
שְׂכָרְךָ הַרְבֵּה מְאֹד: the infinitive absolute הַרְבֵּה in predicate position, with the adverb מְאֹד, gives 'your reward is very great'.
segments.note: 'After these things' keeps the time general; Rashi takes it as 'right after' the defeat of the kings (see commentary). 'In a vision' follows Ibn Ezra. 'I am your shield' is read as protection from the kings (Ibn Ezra, Sforno, Radak), not from punishment for the killings (Rashi, declined). The Hebrew is present tense; the past tense of Ibn Ezra is recorded in the apparatus. 'Your reward is very great' keeps מְאֹד as the Hebrew does; Radak and Sforno read the reward as great in this world and very great in the world to come, which the English leaves open.

commentary.summary: Rashi takes אַחַר as 'right after' the rescue from the kings, when Abram feared he had been paid for his merits, and reads 'shield' as protection from punishment for the men he killed (מִן הָעֹנֶשׁ). The English keeps the time general and reads the shield as protection from the kings.
Ibn Ezra glosses בַּמַּחֲזֶה as 'in visions of prophecy' (במראות הנבואה). The English 'in a vision' follows him.

Ibn Ezra reads 'I am your shield' as 'I was your shield and saved you from the kings', and the reward as owed for Abram's willingness to save his kinsman with few men. The English follows the shield against the kings; the tense is kept as the Hebrew has it, and the past is recorded in the apparatus.

apparatus: 15:1.14-16: Ibn Ezra reads 'I was your shield' (past); the English keeps the present of MAM.

segments.english: Abram said: Lord, the LORD, what will you give me? I go childless, and the steward of my house is Eliezer of Damascus.
segments.literal: and-said Abram; Lord the-LORD; what you-will-give to-me; and-I going childless; and-son possession-of my-house; he Damascus Eliezer.

tokens.note: Vocative of אֲדֹנָי, joined to the divine name; the English keeps both terms: 'Lord, the LORD'.
Yiqtol, second person: a question in the speaker's voice, addressed to the LORD.
BDB gives 'walk, live' (Qal II.2) and 'die' (Qal II.1). Ramban reads 'die'; the plain sense is 'go'.
Literally 'son'. The English 'steward' is an interpretive rendering (see note).
Construct of מֶשֶׁק, 'acquisition, possession'.
Household, as the sense of בַּיִת used with 'possession'.

phrases.english: and the steward of my house

grammar: וַיֹּאמֶר begins the speech: a wayyiqtol that carries the narrative forward. Abram's words follow, with no quotation marks in the English; the colon marks the speech.
אֲדֹנָי יֱהֹוִה is a vocative: 'Lord, the LORD'. The divine name is pointed with the Masoretic vowels of the name, and the English marks it in capitals.
מַה־תִּתֶּן־לִי: an interrogative with a second-person yiqtol, 'what will you give me?', in which Abram addresses the LORD.

וְאָנֹכִי הוֹלֵךְ עֲרִירִי is a circumstantial clause: the independent pronoun and the participle, 'and I go childless'. The etnaḥta on עֲרִירִי divides the question from the statement about the steward.
וּבֶן מֶשֶׁק בֵּיתִי הוּא דַּמֶּשֶׂק אֱלִיעֶזֶר is a nominal clause; הוּא is the copula, 'is'.
segments.note: בֶן מֶשֶׁק בֵּיתִי is literally 'son of the possession of my house'. The English 'steward' follows Rashi (אַפּוֹטְרוֹפּוֹס) and Ibn Ezra, who reads meshek as from a root for busy movement within the house; both make Eliezer the one who runs the household. 'Of Damascus' follows Rashi's reading of the Targum (from Damascus). The literal line keeps 'son'. Radak's sense that this man would inherit if Abram had no son is carried into the English of 15:3, where the same figure appears.

commentary.summary: Rashi glosses עֲרִירִי as 'without an heir, childless' (בְלֹא יוֹרֵשׁ, חֲסַר בָּנִים) and links the word to a root for emptying out. The English 'childless' follows him.

Rashi reads בֶּן מֶשֶׁק בֵּיתִי as the Targum does: the whole household is fed by his word, a steward (אַפּוֹטְרוֹפּוֹס) of mine, and if I had a son, my son would be set over my property. The English 'steward of my house' follows him.
Rashi says that by the Targum Eliezer was from Damascus, and that by the Midrash Abram pursued the kings as far as Damascus. The English 'of Damascus' takes the place-sense that both readings share.
Ibn Ezra explains the form of עֲרִירִי by comparison with Lev 20:21 (ערירים יהיו), and gives it the sense the Targum gives: childless. The English follows him.

Ibn Ezra derives משק from a root for busy movement (שוקק בו), which agrees with the steward sense of Rashi, but he reads בֶן מֶשֶׁק בֵּיתִי as 'the son of Damascus, Eliezer'. The English does not adopt the Damascene reading of 'son'.

apparatus: 15:2.15: Targum Onkelos reads 'the Damascene' (דַּמַּשְׂקָאָה); Radak allows 'Damascene' or that the name was Damascus. The English keeps 'of Damascus'.

segments.english: Abram said: What use is it to me, since you have given no offspring? And look, the steward of my house will inherit from me.
segments.literal: and-said Abram; what-use to-me; not you-have-given offspring; and-look son of-my-house inheriting me.

tokens.note: הֵן is read by Rashi as 'what use is it?' (rashi:15:3:1), not as 'behold'. BDB gives 'lo, behold' for the particle; the English follows Rashi.
Qatal, second person: a complaint about what the LORD has not done.
Rendered 'the steward' as in 15:2.
Participle with future sense: 'will inherit'.
Object suffix with the verb 'inherit'; the object marker has no English counterpart.

phrases.english: What use is it to me
And look, the steward of my house

grammar: הֵן לִי לֹא נָתַתָּה זָרַע: the particle הֵן with לִי is a rhetorical question on Rashi's reading; the qatal נָתַתָּה is the complaint about what the LORD has not given.
The etnaḥta on זָ֑רַע divides the complaint from the statement about the heir.
וְהִנֵּה ... יוֹרֵשׁ אֹתִי: the particle הִנֵּה introduces the participle יוֹרֵשׁ with future sense, 'will inherit'.
The object marker אֹתִי is the first-person suffix with the verb, so the English 'inherit from me' is a direct object with the preposition.
The accents divide the verse into two parts, the complaint and the statement about the house-son.
segments.note: Rashi (rashi:15:3:1) reads הֵן לִי as 'what profit is there in all you give me?', and the English follows him in 'What use is it to me'. The 'steward' is kept from 15:2 so that the figure is the same. Radak (not normative) reads the sentence as an accusation that the LORD has given no seed; that is recorded here only as a neighbouring reading.

commentary.summary: Rashi glosses הֵן לִי לֹא נָתַתָּה זָרַע as 'what profit is there in all that you give me?' (וּמַה תּוֹעֶלֶת בְּכָל אֲשֶׁר תִּתֵּן לִי?). The English 'What use is it to me, since you have given no offspring' follows him.

segments.english: And look, the word of the LORD came to him, saying: This one will not inherit from you, but the one who comes out of your body, he will inherit from you.
segments.literal: and-look word-of the-LORD to-him to-say [came]; not will-inherit-you this-one; but if; who comes-out from-your-body; he will-inherit-you.

tokens.note: כִּי אִם is a restrictive idiom, 'but' or 'only'.
מֵעֶה, 'bowels'. Ibn Ezra: a figure for the organ, because it is near. The English keeps the euphemism.

phrases.english: And look, the word of the LORD came to him, saying
This one will not inherit from you
the one who comes out of your body

grammar: לֹא יִירָשְׁךָ זֶה: a negative yiqtol, third person, 'this one will not inherit from you'; the suffix ךָ is the object.
כִּי־אִם: 'but' in the restrictive idiom 'not X, but Y'. The pashta on אִם marks the break.
אֲשֶׁר יֵצֵא: the relative 'who' with a yiqtol, 'who comes out'.
הוּא יִירָשֶׁךָ: the independent pronoun repeats the subject for emphasis, and sets the second heir against 'this one'.
The silluq on יִירָשֶׁךָ closes the verse on the contrast.
segments.note: 'Your body' keeps the euphemism of מִמֵּעֶיךָ ('from your bowels'), as Ibn Ezra explains it. 'This one' is the house-son of 15:3, and the verse answers that complaint: the heir will be the one from Abram's body. The verse does not say a child is born in this verse.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra explains מִמֵּעֶיךָ as a figure for the organ, because it is near (כנוי לאבר בעבור היותו קרוב). The English 'from your body' keeps the euphemism and follows him.

segments.english: He brought him outside and said: Look now toward the heavens, and count the stars, if you are able to count them. And he said to him: So shall your offspring be.
segments.literal: and-brought-out him outside; and-said; look now to-the-heavens; and-count the-stars; if you-are-able to-count them; and-said to-him; so will-be your-offspring.

tokens.note: Object marker with the third-person suffix.
Imperative of נָבַט, 'look'.
Exhortative particle נָא, 'please, now'.
Object marker with the third-person masculine plural suffix.

phrases.english: if you are able to count them

grammar: וַיּוֹצֵא אֹתוֹ הַחוּצָה: a Hiph wayyiqtol, 'and he brought him outside'; הַחוּצָה is the directional form of 'outside'.
הַבֶּט־נָא: the Hiph imperative of 'look', with the exhortative נָא; the English 'Look now'.
אִם־תּוּכַל לִסְפֹּר: a conditional clause, 'if you are able to count', with the infinitive construct לִסְפֹּר.
כֹּה יִהְיֶה זַרְעֶךָ: the adverb כֹּה 'so' with a yiqtol and the subject after the verb, 'so shall your offspring be'.
The zaqef qaton on לוֹ and the etnaḥta on אֹתָ֑ם divide the act, the command, and the promise.
segments.note: The plain sense (rashi:15:5:1) is that the LORD brought Abram out of his tent to see the stars; the English follows this. Rashi's midrashic reading, that Abram should leave astrology because he will have no son and Abraham will, is not adopted in the English, though it is noted in the commentary.

commentary.summary: Rashi's plain sense (לְפִי פְּשׁוּטוֹ) is that he took him out of the tent to look at the stars (הוֹצִיאוֹ מֵאָהֳלוֹ לַחוּץ לִרְאוֹת הַכּוֹכָבִים). The English 'He brought him outside' and 'Look now toward the heavens' follow the plain sense. The midrashic reading, 'leave your astrology' (צֵא מֵאִצְטַגְנִינוּת שֶׁלְּךָ), is not adopted.

segments.english: He believed in the LORD, and the LORD counted it to him as righteousness.
segments.literal: and-believed in-the-LORD; and-counted it [the LORD] to-him; righteousness.

tokens.note: Variant vowels of the divine name: see apparatus.
Wayyiqtol with the third-person feminine suffix (it, the faith). The subject is not written; the English supplies 'the LORD' with Rashi and the other normative readings.
BDB sense 6, 'justification', is also possible here.

phrases.english: and the LORD counted it to him as righteousness

grammar: וְהֶאֱמִן בַּיהוָה: a Hiph qatal of אָמַן, 'he believed in', with the preposition ב; the sense is trust in the LORD.
וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ: a wayyiqtol with the object suffix הָ. The subject is unwritten; the English supplies 'the LORD' on Rashi's reading.
צְדָקָה is a feminine noun in the absolute state, 'righteousness'.
The tipḥa on וְהֶאֱמִן and the merkha on וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ divide the verse; the silluq on צְדָקָה closes it.
segments.note: The subject of וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ is not written. Rashi, Ramban, Radak and Sforno all take the LORD as the one who counts the faith to Abram, and the English follows them. Rashi's second reading (the merit of the sacrifices, in answer to 'by what shall I know') is recorded in the commentary but not adopted here, because 15:8 is spoken by Abram, not by the verse's narrator.

commentary.summary: Rashi says that Abram did not ask for a sign for this belief (לֹא שָׁאַל לוֹ אוֹת עַל זֹאת); he asked for a sign about inheriting the land. The English 'He believed in the LORD' takes no sign.

Rashi takes the subject to be the Holy One, who counted the faith to Abram as merit and righteousness (חֲשָׁבָהּ לְאַבְרָם לִזְכוּת וְלִצְדָקָה). The English 'and the LORD counted it to him as righteousness' follows him.
Ibn Ezra compares צדקה with Deut 6:25 (וּצְדָקָה תִּהְיֶה לָנוּ), where the word means the righteous standing that comes from the commandment. The English 'righteousness' follows this plain sense.

apparatus: 15:6.2: the WLC vowels read בַּיהוָה; the base text reads בַּיהֹוָה. The English is the same either way.

segments.english: He said to him: I am the LORD, who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans to give you this land to inherit it.
segments.literal: and-said to-him; I the-LORD; who brought-you-out from-Ur the-Chaldeans; to-give to-you the-land this; to-inherit-it.

tokens.note: The verb 'am' is not written; the English supplies it.
The object marker has no English counterpart.

phrases.english: who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans

grammar: אֲנִי יְהוָה: the self-identification formula, 'I am the LORD'; the copula is not written.
הוֹצֵאתִיךָ: a Hiph qatal of יָצָא, 'I brought you out', with the second-person suffix.
לָתֶת לְךָ: an infinitive construct with the preposition, 'to give you', giving the purpose of the bringing out.
לְרִשְׁתָּהּ: an infinitive construct with the third-feminine suffix, 'to inherit it', for the land.
The etnaḥta on אֵלָיו marks the division between the narrator's 'He said to him' and the divine speech.
segments.note: Ur of the Chaldeans is the familiar English for כַּשְׂדִּים; the place name Ur is kept. Ibn Ezra (cross-reference, not a reading) notes that the command is stated in Lekh Lekha and not at Haran. The English 'to inherit it' keeps the inheritance vocabulary of 15:3-4.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra cross-refers to the parashah of Lekh Lekha (12:1), where the command is stated, and says it is not stated at Haran. This is a cross-reference and does not bear on the plain sense of the English.

Ibn Ezra says Abram believed the promise of a son who would inherit him, and asked for a sign about inheriting the land, as Gideon did (ועל ירושת הארץ בקש אות כאשר עשה גדעון); the request was not a sin. The English keeps the land-inheritance as the subject of the sign in 15:8.

segments.english: He said: Lord, the LORD, how shall I know that I will inherit it?
segments.literal: and-said; Lord; the-LORD; by-what shall-I-know that I-will-inherit-it.

tokens.note: Vocative of אֲדֹנָי.
בַּמָּה, 'by what'; the English 'how' keeps the question.
Yiqtol, first person, with the third-feminine suffix for the land.

grammar: בַּמָּה אֵדַע: 'by what shall I know'; the English 'how shall I know' keeps the question.
כִּי אִירָשֶׁנָּה: 'that I will inherit it', a yiqtol first person with the feminine object suffix for the land.
The zaqef qaton on the divine name divides the address from the question; the silluq on אִירָשֶׁנָּה closes the verse.
The verse answers the promise of 15:7: Abram asks for a sign about the land, not about the son.
segments.note: The question is Abram's, and the commentators divide on what he asks. Radak (not normative) reads it as a doubt whether the land will stay with his descendants forever, since they may sin; the English 'that I will inherit it' leaves that open. Ibn Ezra (15:7:2) reads the question as a request for a sign, as Gideon asked.

commentary.summary: Radak reads the question as a doubt about whether the land would be inherited for ever (אִם יִירָשׁוּהָ לְעוֹלָם), since his descendants might sin and be exiled. The English leaves the duration open; Radak's reading is kept here as an alternative.
